newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Future of HK democracy on the line in Beijing meet.
newsitem.headline: Future of HK democracy on the line in Beijing meet.

text.p: The future of democracy in Hong Kong was put on the line as Beijing's hand-picked advisers met on Thursday to set an electoral framework.

As outgoing Governor Chris Patten warned the world would be watching the result, a group of 150 Chinese and Hong Kong worthies opened a two-day meeting in Beijing to lay out procedures for electing Hong Kong's legislature following the British colony's reversion to China on July 1.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, chairman of the so-called Preparatory Committee, said in his opening speech the electoral system would embody the principles of democracy, fairness and openness, the semi-official China News Service (CNS) reported.
"The procedures should neither favour nor disadvantage any particular group participating in the election," Qian was quoted as saying. But he added the paramount concern was stability.
"The measures should give top priority to the maintenance of Hong Kong's long term prosperity and stability," he said.
Hong Kong already has a fully-elected legislature, but China is scrapping it after the handover and installing in its place a provisional council chosen by a 400-member selection committee.
Fresh polls for a new legislature have been promised within a year after the territory of 6.4 million becomes a Chinese Special Administrative Region.

Speaking in London, Patten said those polls would be the measure by which Hong Kong and the international community would judge Beijing's promises of continued democratic development in the territory beyond the handover.

"People in Hong Kong now know what a fair election is like," he said. "Over a million of them voted in a fair election in 1995, they know what decent elections are like as a benchmark by which they can judge whatever elections follow 1 July."

Patten said the fairness, openness and acceptability of electoral arrangements were the most signal indicators, watched not only by Hong Kong but by the world, of how China's promises about the democratisation of the territory would be carried out.

China refused to recognise those 1995 elections cited by Patten, saying electoral reforms adopted for them violated previous Sino-British understandings. The polls returned the first fully-elected legislature in Hong Kong's history.
As the handover comes closer, China said on Thursday it had formed a foreign ministry team for Hong Kong after Britain hands back the colony, but declined to say who would lead it.
Hong Kong newspapers have tipped China's Ambassador to Britain Jiang Enzhu to head the office, handling foreign affairs matters entrusted to it by the Beijing central government.
Australia agreed to recognise the passports that Hong Kong will issue after the handover, the Hong Kong government said.

Canberra promised it will treat holders of the post-handover passports in the same way as holders of so-called British National Overseas (BNO) passports, which are held by about two million Hong Kong people, a government statement said.
Maintenance of easy travel rights by travel partners is regarded as a crucial vote of confidence in Hong Kong's future.
